source.title: Harmless reward hacks can generalize to misalignment in LLMs

record.file_problem: This is an Alignment Forum post showing the abstract, introduction, and descriptions of main figures, not the full paper. Figure 7's numerical results are not present in the text.
record.tranche_reason: It tests whether a narrow fine-tune generalizes to misaligned free-form answers, using harmless reward-hacking demonstrations rather than the original harmful-task training examples.
record.gate_note: The post reports misalignment evaluations on free-response questions, including shutdown resistance. Reward-hacking task scores and chess results are not rows because they do not measure the unrelated misaligned-answer behavior in the claim. Cherry-picked examples are qualitative, not separate quantified results.
record.test_reason: It fine-tunes GPT-4.1 on harmless reward-hacking demonstrations, a dataset type V2 names. It then measures misaligned free-form answers and shutdown resistance on unrelated questions, scored as in Betley et al.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also stress three points. Misalignment appeared in GPT-4.1, not across all trained models. Its rate was lower than with insecure-code or harmful-advice fine-tunes, though the patterns were similar. Coding-only reward hacking did not produce it.
record.recipe_differences: Uses supervised fine-tuning on harmless reward-hacking demonstrations rather than fine-tuning on harmful task behavior; evaluates unrelated free-form misalignment and shutdown responses.
record.method_sensitivity: The post notes that generalization to emergent misalignment depended on training on a wide variety of reward-hacking tasks: coding-only training did not produce it. Shutdown examples also varied by system prompt, but the post does not report rates by prompt.

fits_no_version.finding: Fine-tuned models generalize to novel reward hacking: preferring lenient graders, rewriting reward functions, and hacking chess 94% of the time.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Narrow harmless reward-hack SFT generalizes to broader reward-seeking behavior.

record.problems: The post is an excerpt rather than the full paper, and Figure 7's numerical results and uncertainty are absent. The reported emergent-misalignment results are described for GPT-4.1; the post says the effect occurs in some cases and is generally lower-rate than with other harmful fine-tunes. Authors also note the tasks are simple and training uses supervised fine-tuning rather than reinforcement learning.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows kept. Reward-hacking metrics and chess outcomes were omitted because they measure reward hacking rather than the unrelated misaligned-answer behavior named in the claim.

untested.parts: Bad medical or financial advice and number-sequence fine-tunes are not run as conditions here. They appear only as comparison references, with no numbers.
No insecure-code fine-tune or secure/educational controls.
Training is SFT on reward-hack demonstrations, not RL. The authors flag this as a limitation.
No seed, coherence-filter or training-dynamics results on misalignment in this excerpt.

record.verdict_notes: The source is an Alignment Forum excerpt of arXiv:2508.17511. All misalignment values are figure-only, so the states rest on the authors' prose. The full paper should be read to fill in the rows and the other models' results.

versions.untested_parts: Does not compare insecure-code fine-tuning with secure-code or class-requested insecure-code controls.
Tests harmless reward-hacking fine-tuning, not the other listed datasets such as bad medical or financial advice and number sequences.
Uses supervised fine-tuning, not reinforcement learning.
Does not test a shared direction or persona feature as a mediator.
Does not test inoculation framing or benign retraining as a mitigation.
Does not report misalignment results across model sizes, seeds, coherence filters, or training checkpoints. The described bootstrap runs concern reward-hacking evaluations.
